turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on through. Mind the step. The back's been the problem, has it?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, the bottom of my back. It's really getting to me, doctor. I keep thinking it's something awful.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm Priya, his wife. He only came because I booked it. He's been hobbling round the house.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thanks for coming in with him. How long has the pain been going on?
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): A few weeks. Or since we moved, actually. The move was around Diwali, or just after, I couldn't swear which.
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Longer than that. It was there before Christmas. Three months, easy.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): It wasn't the same pain. Before the move it was a niggle after a shift. The proper pain started when we were hauling boxes.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): So I'm hearing two versions. It might be a few weeks, or it might be nearer three months, and we won't pin the start date today. Where does it sit?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Low down, mostly the right side, going into the buttock. Not down the leg. Is buttock pain a bad sign?
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not on its own, no. How does it feel, what sets it off, and does anything ease it?

[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Right in the low back, going into the buttock. It's a deep ache, sharp if I lift a parcel or sit in the van, and turning in bed sets it off. Walking about eases it, then it comes back. Some days it's an eight out of ten, and I lie there picturing a wheelchair.
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And he still does overtime. Six days, sometimes.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I have to, the mortgage doesn't stop. Should I be signed off? I can't just sit at home, can I?
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll get to work in a minute. First I need to check a few serious things, one by one. Any numbness or tingling in the legs or feet?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): And your waterworks? Trouble starting, leaking, not sensing when the bladder's full?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that's all normal. Same as always.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bowels? New constipation, or any accidents?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Bowels are fine. Nothing new.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any weight loss you didn't intend?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think so. The jeans are looser, but I got a new belt after the move and I've been skipping lunch on early shifts. That isn't really weight loss, is it?
[SEG0022] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He is thinner. His work shirts hang off him. I've had to take the trousers in.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the belt, Priya. I'm not wasting away. Doctor, if I have lost a bit, is that cancer? Just say it.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Unexplained weight loss is a red flag, yes, but skipped lunches and a new belt aren't a measured loss, and the two of you don't agree. I'm not calling this cancer.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever, shivers, night sweats?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever, and no night sweats. I feel worn out, but that's the shifts.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does the pain wake you and keep you awake, or only when you turn?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Only when I turn. I'm not awake at three in agony. Night pain means a tumour, doesn't it? I've been reading.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pain that only comes on turning is much less worrying than pain that builds while you lie still. Any previous back trouble, any X-rays or scans?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): They X-rayed my back at the urgent treatment centre. Said it was borderline, a bit of wear and tear. Last winter, or the winter before, I can't get it straight.
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It was after he slipped on the ice by the warehouse. They didn't give a number, just that word, borderline.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): What does borderline mean? Is the spine crumbling? Have I had arthritis all this time and nobody wrote to me?

[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Borderline isn't a figure I can use, and the report isn't here. Wear-and-tear language is usually ordinary age-related change, not a tumour, and I can't confirm it from memory. What are you taking for the pain?
[SEG0034] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ibuprofen. The 400 milligram tablets, three times a day, every single day. I see him take them.

[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): That's not right. I take one tablet when it's bad, not three times a day, and some days I take none. I'm not even sure they're 400s. Might be the 200s. The box is at home.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any heartburn with them? Asthma, kidney disease, blood thinners?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Heartburn if I take them without food. No asthma, nothing wrong with my kidneys, no blood thinners. Is the heartburn dangerous?
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's a reason not to take anti-inflammatories on an empty stomach. Anything else you use?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol from the cupboard, the 500 milligram tablets. Two of them, sometimes, if the ibuprofen isn't enough. Not every day.
[SEG0040] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And the walk-in doctor gave you codeine. You never took it.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't. My brother was dopey on codeine, so I never started the packet. Should I have? Is that why this hasn't gone?
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): No. Leaving it unopened was reasonable, and I'm not starting codeine today. Any allergies, to medicines or anything else?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No allergies. If I took a few codeine, would I get hooked? I read that too.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): If people take it for weeks it can become habit-forming, which is another reason to leave it. Let me have a look. Stand up and bend forward, slowly.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Like this? Ow. That's the sharp bit. Is that the disc actually going?
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): You only get about halfway forward. The muscles just to the right of the lower spine are tender. I'll lift each straight leg. Tell me if pain shoots down.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): That's a pull in the back, not shooting. Same on both sides. Why the leg thing?
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Straight leg raise doesn't bring on nerve pain on either side. The tender spot feels muscular, which is reassuring.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Wait, about the numbness. I said no earlier, but my left toes go dead when I've been sat in the van. I didn't think that counted. It's not the whole leg.
[SEG0050] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He stamps that foot when he gets out. I thought it was cramp.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Only the left toes? Any weakness, dragging the foot, trouble on the stairs?

[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Just the left toes. It came on sometime in the last week, maybe a bit longer, I can't date it. No weakness. I can still walk on my toes. If they're numb, is the nerve wrecked for good?
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Numbness after sitting often settles, and it doesn't mean permanent damage. Any numbness between the legs, round the saddle, or in the groin?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Definitely not there. That's the emergency one, isn't it? I was up at two reading about it.

[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Saddle numbness with bladder trouble is the emergency pattern, and that isn't what you've described. Overall I think this is mechanical low back pain, though the toe symptoms mean I can't fully exclude a bit of nerve irritation.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): So is it a slipped disc? Am I going to be paralysed? Will I need an operation?

[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): A small disc bulge can irritate a nerve, and plenty settle without an operation. Nothing you've told me points to paralysis. I'm not calling it a slipped disc as a fact, and surgery isn't on the table.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): And that borderline X-ray, you're sure it wasn't the start of a cancer? They never even wrote to me.

[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): I can't re-read a film we haven't got. That wording isn't how a tumour is usually reported. If we need pictures later, it would be a new scan, not a guess off the old one.
[SEG0060] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Can he just have the MRI now? I'll pay if the NHS wait is daft. I don't like this toe business.
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't arrange a lumbar MRI today. If the numbness spreads, a leg gets weak, or this hasn't settled over the next few weeks, then we might request one.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): How many weeks is that? I'm 47 and I pick parcels in a warehouse. If I can't lift, do I just lose the job?
[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): For the next fortnight, no heavy lifting and no overtime, if they'll give you light duties. Do keep walking. Staying in bed makes a back stiffer.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): Heat or ice? And those YouTube stretches, I tried one and panicked I'd snap something.
[SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heat over the sore muscles is fine. Leave the dramatic twists. I'll refer you to physiotherapy so someone watches you move.
[SEG0066] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He won't chase a letter. If you don't send it, it won't happen.

[SEG0067] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll send the physio referral today. For the pain I'll start naproxen, 500 milligrams twice a day, by mouth, with food, for two weeks. Stop the ibuprofen while you're on it. You can keep using paracetamol, two 500 milligram tablets up to four times a day, with a gap.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): Naproxen ruined my uncle's stomach, and I've already got heartburn. Am I going to land in hospital? Do I take it on a good day as well?

[SEG0069] person_1 (DOCTOR): Take both doses with food for the full two weeks, better days included, then we stop and review. If the heartburn turns severe, the stools go black, or you can't keep tablets down, stop the naproxen and ring us the same day. Don't combine it with ibuprofen.
[SEG0070] person_2 (PATIENT): Can I still drive the van? And are the numb toes an A&E job tonight? I nearly went last Sunday and bottled it.

[SEG0071] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you can feel the pedals and do an emergency stop, driving is reasonable. Numb toes on their own are not A&E tonight. Come here or go to A&E the same day if you cannot pass urine, the saddle area goes numb, or a leg gives way.
[SEG0072] person_2 (PATIENT): And if it's just this same ache, when do I come back? I'll spiral if nobody's checking. Should I weigh myself every morning so we catch the weight thing?

[SEG0073] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back if it's not better in three weeks, and sooner if the numbness is spreading. No need for a daily weight chart. If your clothes keep getting obviously looser even though you're eating, tell us.

spec.situation: Manual worker or office worker with low back pain for 'a few weeks or since the move'; doctor asks about red flags (numbness, bladder, weight loss, fever) one by one; patient answers some clearly, some vaguely or with a story. Painkiller use mentioned.
features: vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

bad.reason: Warehouse parcel work supported; lifting parcels not explicitly stated as job duty.
bad.text: occupation (description=Picks and lifts parcels in a warehouse, status=current, reported_by=patient)

Previous back pain before the move was milder: 'a niggle after a shift'; the more severe current pain started while hauling boxes during the move.
Low back pain quality includes a deep ache with sharp pain on lifting or sitting in the van.

Ibuprofen dose/use is recorded incompletely: wife reported 400 mg three times daily every day, but patient said he takes one tablet only when bad, some days none, and is unsure whether they are 200 mg or 400 mg tablets.
Codeine had previously been prescribed by a walk-in doctor, but the patient never started it; doctor advised not starting codeine today.
Paracetamol frequency limit was omitted from current medication details: patient takes two 500 mg tablets sometimes and not every day.
No allergies to medicines or anything else.
Examination detail omitted: straight leg raise caused only a pull in the back, with no shooting pain, same on both sides.
